page: Google Cloud Platform n1-highcpu-8 is an x86_64 architecture server instance belonging to the legacy n1 family. It features 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 4 physical Intel Xeon cores with hyperthreading enabled, operating at a base clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The processor includes a 45 MB L3 cache, 32 KB L1d cache, and 0.25 MB L2 cache, with support for AVX, AES, BMI2, and FMA instructions, though it lacks AVX-512 capabilities. The instance is configured with 7.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-core ratio of approximately 0.9 GB per vCPU. No local storage or GPUs are bundled with this configuration, and it includes zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data indicates that the n1-highcpu-8 delivers modest performance, with many metrics falling into the lower percentiles. The stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU tests register scores of 1109.79 and 5820.12 respectively, placing them in the bottom 25% of tested hardware. Similarly, single-threaded gzip compression at 19.07 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression at 7.0 GB/sec are in the bottom 10%. However, the instance achieves average performance in specific workloads, such as Geekbench ray tracing at 6021.0 and PassMark CPU score at 6786.78. Memory bandwidth for large uncached blocks is also average, with read speeds at 47.28 GB/sec and write speeds at 34.7 GB/sec, though small-block cached reads fall into the bottom 25% at 325.55 GB/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the n1-highcpu-8 offers a low-cost entry point for multi-core compute workloads that do not require high memory density. The primary tradeoff is the highly constrained memory capacity of 7.0 GB, which limits its suitability for memory-intensive applications or large databases, as reflected in the weak PassMark database operations score of 2431.16. Additionally, the lack of local storage requires external block storage attachments. This instance is best suited for compute-bound tasks with small memory footprints, such as basic software compilation, lightweight ray tracing, or text generation using small language models, where it achieves an average text generation speed of 99.37 tokens/second for a 135M model.
